text: Most people take supplements for one
reason, to protect their health. But
what many people don't realize is that
some of the most popular supplements out
there may be doing more harm than good.
I'm Dr. Mitch Rice, a practicing
board-certified primary care physician
in the United States, and in today's
video, I'm going to walk you through the
five most popular supplements that I
recommend stopping and what to do
instead. The first supplement that we're
talking about today is potassium
supplements. Potassium is essential.
Your heart depends on it, your muscles
use it, your nerves need it to send
signals, and potassium plays an
important role in blood pressure
control. So when people hear that
potassium helps lower blood pressure,
they assume more is better. But that's
where the problem starts. Unlike
potassium from food, potassium
supplements deliver a concentrated dose
all at once. And for some people, that
can be dangerous. Here's why. Many blood
pressure medications already raise
potassium levels. These include things
like ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and
potassium-sparing diuretics. If someone
adds a potassium supplement on top of
one of these medications, potassium
levels can raise too high. High
potassium doesn't just cause mild
symptoms. It can cause heart rhythm
problems, muscle weakness, and in severe
cases, cardiac arrest, better known as
your heart completely stopping. And the
scary part is you may not feel anything
at all until something serious happens.
Now this doesn't mean that potassium
supplements for everyone is bad, as in
certain patients for blood pressure
control, I do recommend taking
potassium. But the thing I try to push
more often is that potassium from food
is better than potassium from
supplements. Foods like beans, bananas,
leafy greens, avocados, and potatoes,
these deliver potassium slowly along
with fiber and other nutrients that help
regulate the body properly. The bottom
line is this, potassium is important,
potassium supplements can be a little
risky, and potassium from food is the
safer choice for most people. This is
the one supplement that I always want to
see patients labs before recommending.
Now, potassium isn't the only mineral
that people tend to overdo. Let's talk
about the one that's been recommended
for decades, and that is calcium.
Calcium is vital. Your bones store it,
your heart uses it to beat, and your
muscles use it to contract. Now, as we
mature in life, bone loss becomes a real
problem, especially for older adults and
postmenopausal women. So, it feels
logical to take a calcium supplement.
But, here's the part many people don't
realize. When calcium comes in the form
of a pill, it enters the bloodstream
very quickly. The sudden rise in blood
calcium appears to increase the risk of
calcium settling where it doesn't
belong, including the inside of artery
walls. Multiple large studies have shown
that people taking calcium supplements
had higher rates of heart attacks
compared to those who didn't. The risk
seems even higher when calcium is taken
without enough vitamin D. This does not
mean that calcium is harmful, but it
means, once again, the source matters.
Calcium from food is absorbed slowly and
steadily, whereas calcium from
supplements arrives like a surge, and
arteries don't do well with surges.
Foods rich in calcium include dairy,
sardines, leafy greens, and fortified
foods.
These come packaged with other nutrients
that help calcium go where it's supposed
to go, into the bones and not the
arteries. The bottom line is this,
calcium is essential, calcium
supplements are often the problem, and
calcium from food is significantly
safer. For most people, food first is
the better strategy. Supplement three is
one that most people start taking
without ever checking their labs in the
first place, and that is iron. Iron
carries oxygen to your blood. Without
enough iron, people feel tired, weak,
and foggy. So, iron supplements are easy
to reach for, but iron, like much of
human physiology, follows what we call
the Goldilocks principle. Too little
iron causes problems, but too much iron
also causes problems as well. The body
works best when iron levels are just
right. Excess iron increases oxidative
stress, inflammation, and causes damage
to organs like the liver and the heart.
And unlike some minerals, the body has
no easy way to remove extra iron. So,
when levels get too high, iron will
build up over time. Now, the key thing
that I want you to take away from iron
supplements is this, most adult men and
postmenopausal women do not need extra
iron unless a deficiency is proven. How
do we prove that a deficiency is there?
By getting blood work. Taking iron for
just in case or because you're feeling a
little bit tired can do more harm than
good. Again, like everything we've
talked about so far, iron is much safer
if it's taken in from food sources. The
best sources of iron from food are from
animal sources like red meat because the
iron is absorbed more efficiently. Plant
sources can work, but absorption is
slower. Now, there are people who
absolutely need iron supplementation,
and these are usually pregnant women,
people with heavy amounts of blood loss,
and individuals with certain digestive
conditions. The bottom line is this,
iron is essential, extra iron can
definitely be harmful, and supplements
should only follow lab confirmation of
iron deficiency. Now, let's talk about
the supplement that was once prescribed
to fix bad cholesterol. Supplement
number four on our list is niacin, also
known as vitamin B3. Niacin used to be
very popular in heart care. It lowers
LDL cholesterol, and it can raise HDL
cholesterol. And on paper, this looks
wonderful, but there's one major
problem. When researchers looked at
actual outcomes, niacin didn't reduce
heart attacks or strokes, and it came
with some real side effects. High doses
of niacin increases the risk of liver
injury, worsening blood sugar control,
and generalized flushing. In other
words, it improves lab numbers, but it
doesn't actually improve health
outcomes. This is actually such an
important lesson. Lowering a number on
paper doesn't mean lowering real-world
risk. I'll say that again, and I try to
emphasize this to my patients, is that I
am treating the person in front of me,
not just their lab values. Too many
times, it's easy to get caught up in the
numbers and not looking at the person in
front of you. Today, niacin is rarely
recommended for cardiovascular concerns.
For most people, it adds risk without
much benefit. The bottom line is this,
niacin changes cholesterol numbers, but
it does not improve real-world outcomes.
The risks often outweigh the benefits.
And finally, let's talk about the fifth
most popular supplement that I see and
often tell patients to stop, and that is
turmeric or curcumin. Turmeric has
become one of the most popular
supplements for longevity and joint
health. It's often promoted as a
powerful anti-inflammatory agent, a
protector against aging, and a natural
way to support the heart and the brain.
And the idea sounds great. Less
inflammation should mean better health
outcomes. But when we look closely at
human research, the story gets a bit
more complicated.
While turmeric from food is safe and
traditional, high doses of curcumin
supplements, which is the active
ingredient in turmeric, don't always act
the way that people expect. In some
studies, large doses of curcumin appear
to blunt the body's natural stress
response. And this matters because a
little stress is how the body actually
gets stronger. Exercise works by
creating small amounts of stress that
signal cells to repair, adapt, and
become more resilient. High doses of
antioxidant supplements can block that
signal. In other words, you may be
canceling out part of the benefit of
exercise, especially strength training
and cardiovascular training, without
realizing it. Now, there's also another
concern with curcumin. These supplements
can interact with certain blood-thinning
medications, affect liver enzymes, and
cause significant nausea and digestion
upset at higher doses. And despite all
the hype, we don't actually have good
evidence that curcumin supplements
extend lifespan, prevent heart disease,
or meaningfully improve long-term health
outcomes. If you want to use turmeric as
a spice food, that's totally fine. But
if you want to take high doses of
curcumin every day, that's not as
harmless as it sounds. The bottom line
is this, turmeric supplements don't
reliably deliver longevity benefits,
high doses may interfere with exercise
adaptation, and food sources are safer,
whereas supplements deserve caution.
Healthy aging doesn't come from blocking
every stress signal possible, it comes
